### Show the distributions of values visually. Explain, in comments, what those distributions mean statistically. Be thorough.
```{r}
# path is hard coded to dataset, can easily replace with your path
data <- read.csv("/Users/gvance67/GitHub/data_science_classes/term 2/DSC520 - Statistics for Data Science/week 2/sales_data_sample.csv") 
library(dplyr)


# display the first 6 rows of the data
head(data)

# print each column with its type - str is structure of data
str(data)

# This task is fairly open ended, but we can do a few things. We can loop through all regions and show products. This would merely give us product rows. Then we can weight the rows by multiplying the quantity. This would show to what degree the products are purchased throughout the regions


south_data <- data %>% filter(Region == "South")
north_data <- data %>% filter(Region == "North")
east_data <- data %>% filter(Region == "East")
west_data <- data %>% filter(Region == "West")

south_products <- table(south_data$Product)
north_products <- table(north_data$Product)
east_products <- table(east_data$Product)
west_products <- table(west_data$Product)



pie(south_products, 
    labels = names(south_products), 
    col = rainbow(length(south_products)), 
    main = "Southern Region Product Distribution")

pie(north_products, 
    labels = names(north_products), 
    col = rainbow(length(north_products)), 
    main = "Northern Region Product Distribution")

pie(east_products, 
    labels = names(east_products), 
    col = rainbow(length(east_products)), 
    main = "Eastern Region Product Distribution")

```
